pos: n. (the goddess of Ephesus, whose silver trade rioted against Paul; Greek Artemis)
etymology: Latin Diana, the KJV's rendering of Greek Artemis. The Ephesian Artemis was not the huntress of the poets but a many-breasted fertility image, housed in one of the wonders of the ancient world.
biblical_def: The riot at Ephesus begins in a workshop: “a certain man named Demetrius, a silversmith, which made silver shrines for Diana, brought no small gain unto the craftsmen” (Act 19:24). His complaint is that Paul has said “they be no gods, which are made with hands” (Act 19:26). The crowd answers with a chant: “Great is Diana of the Ephesians” (Act 19:28), and again for two hours together (Act 19:34). The townclerk quiets them by appealing to the city's standing as “a worshipper of the great goddess Diana, and of the image which fell down from Jupiter” (Act 19:35).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines an idol as an image or representation consecrated as an object of worship, and a shrine as a case or box in which sacred things are deposited.
webster_full: IDOL, n. An image, form or representation, usually of a man or other animal, consecrated as an object of worship.
SHRINE, n. A case, box or repository in which sacred things are deposited.
GODDESS, n. A female deity; a heathen deity of the female sex.
scriptures: For a certain man named Demetrius, a silversmith, which made silver shrines for Diana, brought no small gain unto the craftsmen;
Moreover ye see and hear, that not alone at Ephesus, but almost throughout all Asia, this Paul hath persuaded and turned away much people, saying that they be no gods, which are made with hands:
And when they heard these sayings, they were full of wrath, and cried out, saying, Great is Diana of the Ephesians.

And when the townclerk had appeased the people, he said, Ye men of Ephesus, what man is there that knoweth not how that the city of the Ephesians is a worshipper of the great goddess Diana, and of the image which fell down from Jupiter?
corruption_summary: Demetrius names his real grievance first — the craft is in danger — and only afterwards remembers the goddess.
corruption_paragraphs: Luke reports the speech in the order Demetrius gave it. Sirs, ye know that by this craft we have our wealth; then, this Paul hath persuaded much people; then, our craft is in danger to be set at nought; and only then, the temple of the great goddess Diana should be despised. The theology is third on the list and arrives as reinforcement. The crowd that took up the cry did not know why they had come together — Luke says so plainly — and shouted one sentence for two hours. Religious outrage in Scripture is very often an economic interest that has found a slogan.

The corruption to name is the use of piety as cover for commerce, which is not an ancient failing only. The New Testament warns repeatedly of men supposing that gain is godliness, of those who through covetousness make merchandise of the flock, of teaching things they ought not for filthy lucre's sake. The test Paul applied at Ephesus was doctrinal and simple: they be no gods, which are made with hands. It cost him a riot, two years of labour, and the sentence in his letter to Corinth about having fought with beasts at Ephesus. And the gospel spread through all Asia anyway.
roots_summary: Greek Artemis (G735), Diana of the Ephesians; naos (G3485), shrine, temple; cheiropoietos (G5499), made with hands.
roots_lines: Greek cheiropoietos (G5499) — made with hands; Acts 19:26, 7:48, Hebrews 9:24.
Greek diopetes (G1356) — fallen from Jupiter; Acts 19:35 only.
usage: “Silver shrines for Diana” — and no small gain unto the craftsmen.
“They be no gods, which are made with hands” — the doctrine that caused the riot.
“Great is Diana of the Ephesians” — two hours, one sentence.

pos: n. (the chief god of the Roman pantheon, Greek Zeus; the name the men of Lystra gave to Barnabas)
etymology: Latin Iuppiter, sky-father, the KJV's rendering of Greek Zeus. Every city of the region kept a temple of Zeus before its gates, which is why a priest was on hand within minutes.
biblical_def: After the healing of the cripple at Lystra, “the people saw what Paul had done, they lifted up their voices, saying in the speech of Lycaonia, The gods are come down to us in the likeness of men” (Act 14:11); “And they called Barnabas, Jupiter; and Paul, Mercurius, because he was the chief speaker” (Act 14:12). “Then the priest of Jupiter, which was before their city, brought oxen and garlands unto the gates, and would have done sacrifice with the people” (Act 14:13). The apostles ran in among them crying, “Sirs, why do ye these things? We also are men of like passions with you” (Act 14:15).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines Jupiter as the supreme deity among the Greeks and Romans, and also the largest of the planets, named from that deity.
webster_full: JUPITER, n. The chief divinity of the ancient Greeks and Romans; the supposed son of Saturn.
JUPITER, n. One of the superior planets, remarkable for its brightness; the largest of the planets.
SACRIFICE, n. An offering made to God, or to a false god, by killing and consuming a victim on an altar.
scriptures: And when the people saw what Paul had done, they lifted up their voices, saying in the speech of Lycaonia, The gods are come down to us in the likeness of men.
And they called Barnabas, Jupiter; and Paul, Mercurius, because he was the chief speaker.
Then the priest of Jupiter, which was before their city, brought oxen and garlands unto the gates, and would have done sacrifice with the people.

And saying, Sirs, why do ye these things? We also are men of like passions with you, and preach unto you that ye should turn from these vanities unto the living God, which made heaven, and earth, and the sea, and all things that are therein:
corruption_summary: Paul and Barnabas tore their clothes to stop a crowd from worshipping them, and the same crowd stoned Paul within the chapter.
corruption_paragraphs: Acts 14 contains the two temptations of ministry in the space of a few verses. First the city tries to sacrifice to them, and the apostles rend their clothes and run in among the people crying, we also are men of like passions with you. Then Jews from Antioch and Iconium arrive, persuade the same crowd, and Paul is stoned and dragged out of the city for dead. Adulation and violence from one population within days. The apostolic response to the first is as vigorous as the endurance of the second: no man who accepts the garlands will survive the stones.

The corruption to name is the veneration of ministers, which Scripture forbids as consistently as it forbids idolatry, because it is idolatry. Peter lifts Cornelius off the floor saying stand up; I myself also am a man. The angel tells John twice, see thou do it not: worship God. Paul asks the Corinthians whether Paul was crucified for them. The Reformed insistence that no man is a mediator, that ministers are servants and not lords over God's heritage, and that no created person receives religious veneration, rests on texts like this one — and on the fact that the men who were offered oxen and garlands were horrified.
roots_summary: Greek Zeus (G2203), Jupiter; Hermes (G2060), Mercurius; homoiopathes (G3663), of like passions.
roots_lines: Greek homoiopathes (G3663) — of like passions, like nature; Acts 14:15, James 5:17.
usage: “The gods are come down to us in the likeness of men” — the cry at Lystra.
“They called Barnabas, Jupiter; and Paul, Mercurius” — and the priest brought oxen.
“We also are men of like passions with you” — the apostolic refusal.

pos: n. (the Sidonian fertility goddess; plural Ashtaroth, the recurring snare of Israel in the Judges)
etymology: Hebrew ashtoreth, the Canaanite Astarte. The Masoretic pointing carries the vowels of bosheth, shame — the scribes would not pronounce the name as its worshippers did.
biblical_def: Ashtoreth is the goddess of the great apostasies. Of Solomon: “Solomon went after Ashtoreth the goddess of the Zidonians, and after Milcom the abomination of the Ammonites” (1Ki 11:5), and the LORD's indictment names her first: “they have forsaken me, and have worshipped Ashtoreth the goddess of the Zidonians” (1Ki 11:33). Josiah destroyed her high places three centuries later (2Ki 23:13). And she is the plural snare of the Judges era: “they forsook the LORD, and served Baal and Ashtaroth” (Jdg 2:13), until Samuel demanded, “put away the strange gods and Ashtaroth from among you… and serve him only” (1Sa 7:3).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines an abomination as that which is abominable, an object of hatred and disgust, and in Scripture uses the word especially of idols and idolatrous practices.
webster_full: ABOMINATION, n. That which is abominable; an object of hatred and disgust. In Scripture, defilement, pollution; also, an idol or idolatrous practice.
GROVE, n. In Scripture, an idolatrous emblem or object of worship, set up beside an altar.
ASTARTE, n. The Syrian goddess of the moon, worshipped also under the name of Ashtoreth.
scriptures: Jdg 2:13
And they forsook the LORD, and served Baal and Ashtaroth.

And Samuel spake unto all the house of Israel, saying, If ye do return unto the LORD with all your hearts, then put away the strange gods and Ashtaroth from among you, and prepare your hearts unto the LORD, and serve him only: and he will deliver you out of the hand of the Philistines.
For Solomon went after Ashtoreth the goddess of the Zidonians, and after Milcom the abomination of the Ammonites.

Because that they have forsaken me, and have worshipped Ashtoreth the goddess of the Zidonians, Chemosh the god of the Moabites, and Milcom the god of the children of Ammon, and have not walked in my ways, to do that which is right in mine eyes, and to keep my statutes and my judgments, as did David his father.
corruption_summary: Samuel's call to put away Ashtaroth ends in three words that fix the whole matter: and serve him only.
corruption_paragraphs: First Samuel 7:3 is the anatomy of repentance in one verse. If ye do return unto the LORD with all your hearts — the whole heart, not a division of it. Then put away the strange gods and Ashtaroth from among you — a definite removal of definite things. Prepare your hearts unto the LORD — an inward work following the outward one. And serve him only — the exclusive clause that makes it worship rather than addition. Israel's sin under the Judges was rarely the abandonment of the LORD; it was the retention of the LORD alongside Baal and Ashtaroth. That is what only is aimed at.

The corruption to name is syncretism, and it is the specific form idolatry takes among people who still consider themselves believers. Solomon did not renounce the God who had appeared to him twice; he built high places for Ashtoreth on the hill before Jerusalem and kept the temple standing. Elijah's question on Carmel assumes the same condition: how long halt ye between two opinions? The first commandment does not forbid preferring the LORD; it forbids having any other gods before Him. Josiah's reform is the model — he defiled the high places Solomon had built, three hundred years after the fact, because a compromise outlives the man who made it.
roots_summary: Hebrew Ashtoreth (H6252), Astarte; Ashtaroth, its plural; shiqquts (H8251), detestable thing, abomination; bad (H905), alone, only.
roots_lines: Hebrew Ashtoreth (H6252) — Ashtoreth, Ashtaroth; Judges 2:13, 1 Samuel 7:3, 1 Kings 11:5, 11:33.
Hebrew shiqquts (H8251) — detestable thing, abomination; 1 Kings 11:5, 2 Kings 23:13.
Hebrew bad (H905) — alone, only, apart; 1 Samuel 7:3, Deuteronomy 6:4.
Hebrew kun (H3559) — to prepare, establish, fix; 1 Samuel 7:3, Psalm 57:7.
usage: “They forsook the LORD, and served Baal and Ashtaroth” — the refrain of Judges.
“Put away the strange gods and Ashtaroth… and serve him only” — Samuel's terms.
“Solomon went after Ashtoreth the goddess of the Zidonians.”

pos: n. (the god of Ekron, consulted by Ahaziah; in the Gospels, Beelzebub, the prince of the devils)
etymology: Hebrew baal zebub, lord of the fly. Whether the Philistines meant it as a title of power over plague-flies or Israel coined it in mockery, the Gospel form Beelzebub carries it forward as a name for Satan himself.
biblical_def: “Ahaziah fell down through a lattice in his upper chamber that was in Samaria, and was sick: and he sent messengers, and said unto them, Go, enquire of Baalzebub the god of Ekron whether I shall recover of this disease” (2Ki 1:2). Elijah is sent to intercept them with a question: “Is it not because there is not a God in Israel, that ye go to enquire of Baalzebub the god of Ekron?” (2Ki 1:3), and to the king in person: “thou shalt not come down off that bed on which thou art gone up, but shalt surely die” (2Ki 1:16). In the Gospels the Pharisees use the name against Christ: “This fellow doth not cast out devils, but by Beelzebub the prince of the devils” (Mat 12:24).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) treats Beelzebub as the name of the god of Ekron, and in the New Testament as a name of the prince of evil spirits.
webster_full: BEELZEBUB, n. The god of flies, an idol of the Ekronites; in the New Testament, the prince of the devils.
ORACLE, n. Among the heathen, the answer of a god or some person reputed to be a god, to an inquiry made respecting some future event.
DIVINATION, n. The act of divining; a foretelling future events, or discovering things secret, by unlawful arts.
scriptures: And Ahaziah fell down through a lattice in his upper chamber that was in Samaria, and was sick: and he sent messengers, and said unto them, Go, enquire of Baalzebub the god of Ekron whether I shall recover of this disease.

But the angel of the LORD said to Elijah the Tishbite, Arise, go up to meet the messengers of the king of Samaria, and say unto them, Is it not because there is not a God in Israel, that ye go to enquire of Baalzebub the god of Ekron?

And he said unto him, Thus saith the LORD, Forasmuch as thou hast sent messengers to enquire of Baalzebub the god of Ekron, is it not because there is no God in Israel to enquire of his word? therefore thou shalt not come down off that bed on which thou art gone up, but shalt surely die.
But when the Pharisees heard it, they said, This fellow doth not cast out devils, but by Beelzebub the prince of the devils.
corruption_summary: Elijah's question is the whole indictment: is it not because there is no God in Israel? The sin was where the king sent, not what he asked.
corruption_paragraphs: Ahaziah's question was reasonable enough — whether he would recover — and God answered it, through Elijah, in the negative. The sin was the address. Is it not because there is not a God in Israel, that ye go to enquire of Baalzebub the god of Ekron? The king of the covenant people, injured in his own house, sent past the prophet in his own land to a Philistine shrine. Saul had done the same at Endor and died the next day. Consulting the dead or the demons is treated in Scripture not merely as futile but as apostasy, because it declares that the LORD either cannot answer or will not.

The corruption to name is the traffic in guidance outside of God's word, from the frank occultism Deuteronomy 18 lists — divination, observing times, enchantment, witchcraft, consulting familiar spirits — to its softer modern forms, which are not less a search for a word from somewhere other than Scripture. Isaiah 8:19-20 gives both the practice and the standard: should not a people seek unto their God? for the living to the dead? To the law and to the testimony: if they speak not according to this word, it is because there is no light in them.
roots_summary: Hebrew baal zebub, lord of the fly; Greek Beelzeboul (G954); Hebrew darash (H1875), to seek, enquire of.
roots_lines: Hebrew Baal zebub (H1176) — Baalzebub, god of Ekron; 2 Kings 1:2, 1:3, 1:6, 1:16.
Hebrew darash (H1875) — to seek, enquire, consult; 2 Kings 1:2, Deuteronomy 18:11.
Hebrew Eqron (H6138) — Ekron, a Philistine city; 2 Kings 1:2, 1 Samuel 5:10.
usage: “Go, enquire of Baalzebub the god of Ekron” — the king's message.
“Is it not because there is not a God in Israel?” — Elijah's question.
“By Beelzebub the prince of the devils” — the charge against Christ.

pos: n. (son of Cush; the first man Scripture calls mighty, and the founder of Babel)
etymology: Hebrew Nimrod, traditionally connected with marad, to rebel. Genesis says he began to be a mighty one in the earth, and the kingdom he began was Babel.
biblical_def: “And Cush begat Nimrod: he began to be a mighty one in the earth” (Gen 10:8). “He was a mighty hunter before the LORD: wherefore it is said, Even as Nimrod the mighty hunter before the LORD” (Gen 10:9). The next verse names what he built: “the beginning of his kingdom was Babel, and Erech, and Accad, and Calneh, in the land of Shinar” (Gen 10:10) — and the following chapter records what was said in that place: “let us build us a city and a tower, whose top may reach unto heaven; and let us make us a name” (Gen 11:4). Chronicles repeats the genealogy (1Ch 1:10), and Micah calls Assyria “the land of Nimrod” (Mic 5:6).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a hunter as one who pursues wild animals with a view to take them, and mighty as very strong, powerful, having great command.
webster_full: HUNTER, n. One who pursues wild animals with a view to take them, either for sport or for food.
MIGHTY, a. Having great bodily strength or physical power; very strong; powerful.
MIGHTY, n. A warrior; a chieftain of great valor or power.
scriptures: Gen 10:8
And Cush begat Nimrod: he began to be a mighty one in the earth.
Gen 10:9
He was a mighty hunter before the LORD: wherefore it is said, Even as Nimrod the mighty hunter before the LORD.
And the beginning of his kingdom was Babel, and Erech, and Accad, and Calneh, in the land of Shinar.
Gen 11:4
And they said, Go to, let us build us a city and a tower, whose top may reach unto heaven; and let us make us a name, lest we be scattered abroad upon the face of the whole earth.
corruption_summary: Nimrod is the first man in Scripture called mighty, the first to have a kingdom, and the founder of the city that becomes the Bible's standing name for organized rebellion.
corruption_paragraphs: Genesis 10:8-10 is short and heavy with consequence. Nimrod began to be a mighty one — a new thing in the earth after the flood — and the beginning of his kingdom was Babel. Genesis is careful with beginnings, and this is the beginning of empire. The stated purpose at Babel is not defence or trade but reputation and cohesion: let us make us a name, lest we be scattered — a direct refusal of the command given to Noah to replenish the earth. Babylon runs from that tower through Nebuchadnezzar to Revelation 18, and Micah still calls Assyria the land of Nimrod centuries later.

The corruption to name is the city that builds upward to make a name for itself, which is the perennial project of human civilization and not a relic of the ancient world. Augustine's two cities are drawn from this material: one founded on the love of God to the contempt of self, the other on the love of self to the contempt of God. God's answer to Babel was not destruction but confusion of language, and the reversal comes at Pentecost, where men out of every nation under heaven hear the wonderful works of God each in his own tongue. Babel gathers to make a name; the gospel scatters in the name that is above every name.
roots_summary: Hebrew gibbor (H1368), mighty one, warrior; tsayid (H6718), hunting, game; Babel (H894), Babel, confusion; shem (H8034), name.
roots_lines: Hebrew gibbor (H1368) — mighty one, champion; Genesis 10:8, 6:4, Psalm 45:3.
Hebrew Shinar (H8152) — Shinar, the plain of Babylonia; Genesis 10:10, Daniel 1:2.
usage: “He began to be a mighty one in the earth” — the first such man named.
“The beginning of his kingdom was Babel” — the beginning of empire.
“Let us make us a name” — the purpose stated at the tower.

pos: n. (Cyprus and the coasts and isles beyond it; the far west of the biblical world)
etymology: Hebrew Kittim, from Kition on Cyprus, and by extension the maritime lands west of it. It is the Old Testament's standing name for whatever lies out past the horizon of the Mediterranean.
biblical_def: Balaam's last oracle reaches to it: “ships shall come from the coast of Chittim, and shall afflict Asshur, and shall afflict Eber, and he also shall perish for ever” (Num 24:24). Tyre's fall is reported to the sailors from there: “from the land of Chittim it is revealed to them” (Isa 23:1), and Zidon is told to flee that way and find no rest (Isa 23:12). Ezekiel puts its timber in Tyre's ships (Eze 27:6). And Jeremiah sends the reader west and east to look for a parallel: “pass over the isles of Chittim, and see; and send unto Kedar, and consider diligently, and see if there be such a thing” (Jer 2:10).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines an isle as a tract of land surrounded by water, and coast as the exterior line, limit, or border of a country, particularly on the sea.
webster_full: ISLE, n. A tract of land surrounded by water, or a detached portion of land embosomed in the ocean.
COAST, n. The exterior line, limit or border of a country, as in Scripture; more usually, the edge or margin of the land next to the sea.
MARITIME, a. Relating to the sea or ocean; as maritime affairs; bordering on the sea.
scriptures: And ships shall come from the coast of Chittim, and shall afflict Asshur, and shall afflict Eber, and he also shall perish for ever.
Isa 23:1
The burden of Tyre. Howl, ye ships of Tarshish; for it is laid waste, so that there is no house, no entering in: from the land of Chittim it is revealed to them.
Jer 2:10
For pass over the isles of Chittim, and see; and send unto Kedar, and consider diligently, and see if there be such a thing.
Jer 2:11
Hath a nation changed their gods, which are yet no gods? but my people have changed their glory for that which doth not profit.
corruption_summary: Jeremiah sends a survey to the ends of the earth and reports that no heathen nation has ever done what Israel did.
corruption_paragraphs: Jeremiah 2:10-11 is one of the most devastating arguments in the prophets, and it is made by comparison with the heathen. Go west to the isles of Chittim, go east to Kedar, look carefully, and see if there be such a thing: has a nation ever changed its gods, which are yet no gods? Pagan peoples keep the deities they inherit even though those deities are nothing. My people have changed their glory for that which doth not profit. Israel is convicted not by a standard the nations met and she failed, but by a loyalty the nations show to lies and she would not show to the truth.

The corruption to name is the low view of apostasy that treats abandoning the faith as an intellectual event with no moral weight. Jeremiah puts it as an exchange — they have forsaken me the fountain of living waters, and hewed them out cisterns, broken cisterns, that can hold no water — and calls the heavens to be astonished at it. The comparison with Chittim and Kedar removes every excuse: the constancy Israel lacked was not a rare virtue but the ordinary conduct of the surrounding world. A people who have known the living God and left Him have done something the pagans never thought to do.
roots_summary: Hebrew Kittim (H3794), Chittim, Cyprus and the western isles; iy (H339), isle, coastland; mur (H4171), to change, exchange.
roots_lines: Hebrew Kittim (H3794) — Chittim; Numbers 24:24, Isaiah 23:1, Jeremiah 2:10, Ezekiel 27:6.
Hebrew mur (H4171) — to change, exchange; Jeremiah 2:11, Psalm 106:20.
Hebrew Qedar (H6938) — Kedar, the eastern nomads; Jeremiah 2:10, Psalm 120:5.
Hebrew yaal (H3276) — to profit, benefit; Jeremiah 2:11, Isaiah 44:9.
usage: “Ships shall come from the coast of Chittim” — Balaam's last oracle.
“Pass over the isles of Chittim, and see” — a survey of the whole world.
“My people have changed their glory for that which doth not profit.”

pos: n. (the African coast west of Egypt; an ally of Egypt and Gog in the prophets, and a homeland of Pentecost hearers)
etymology: Greek Libue, the ancient name for North Africa west of the Nile. The Hebrew behind it is Put or Phut, a son of Ham in the table of nations.
biblical_def: Libya appears in the prophets as a nation that falls with the empire it leaned on: “Ethiopia, and Libya, and Lydia, and all the mingled people, and Chub, and the men of the land that is in league, shall fall with them by the sword” (Eze 30:5), a judgment on Egypt in which “the pride of her power shall come down” (Eze 30:6). It rides in Gog's company as well: “Persia, Ethiopia, and Libya with them; all of them with shield and helmet” (Eze 38:5). And it stands in the Pentecost roll call: “in Egypt, and in the parts of Libya about Cyrene, and strangers of Rome, Jews and proselytes” (Act 2:10).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a proselyte as a new convert to some religion or religious sect, particularly a convert from paganism to Judaism.
webster_full: PROSELYTE, n. A new convert to some religion, or to some religious sect, or to a particular opinion.
LEAGUE, n. An alliance or confederacy between princes or states for their mutual aid or defense.
CYRENE, n. An ancient city and district of northern Africa, west of Egypt.
scriptures: Eze 30:5
Ethiopia, and Libya, and Lydia, and all the mingled people, and Chub, and the men of the land that is in league, shall fall with them by the sword.
Eze 30:6
Thus saith the LORD; They also that uphold Egypt shall fall; and the pride of her power shall come down: from the tower of Syene shall they fall in it by the sword, saith the Lord GOD.
Eze 38:5
Persia, Ethiopia, and Libya with them; all of them with shield and helmet:
Act 2:10
Phrygia, and Pamphylia, in Egypt, and in the parts of Libya about Cyrene, and strangers of Rome, Jews and proselytes,
corruption_summary: Ezekiel says they that uphold Egypt shall fall with her, which is the standing rule for every alliance made against God's word.
corruption_paragraphs: Ezekiel 30:6 states a principle wider than its occasion: they also that uphold Egypt shall fall. Libya, Ethiopia, Lydia and the men of the land that is in league went down in the judgment of a power they had propped up. The prophets return to this again and again because Judah was constantly tempted to be one of those propping nations — Isaiah 30 pronounces woe on those who go down to Egypt for help, and stay on horses, and look not unto the Holy One of Israel. A confederacy is not neutral. It ties the fortunes of the ally to the judgment already pronounced.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that Acts 2 answers Ezekiel 30. The same Libya about Cyrene that stood in Egypt's doomed league stands in the Pentecost list, hearing the wonderful works of God in its own tongue — and Simon of Cyrene carried the cross, and men of Cyrene were among the first to preach to the Greeks at Antioch. The nations under judgment in the prophets are the nations evangelized in Acts. God's dealings with a people in one century do not fix His dealings with them in the next, and the roll call at Pentecost is deliberately a roll call of old enemies.
roots_summary: Hebrew Put (H6316), Phut, Libya; Greek Libue (G3033); Hebrew gaon (H1347), pride, excellency.
roots_lines: Hebrew Put (H6316) — Phut, Libya; Ezekiel 30:5, 38:5, Genesis 10:6, Nahum 3:9.
Hebrew gaon (H1347) — pride, excellency, majesty; Ezekiel 30:6, Proverbs 16:18.
usage: “They also that uphold Egypt shall fall” — the rule for allies.
“Persia, Ethiopia, and Libya with them” — Gog's company.
“The parts of Libya about Cyrene” — and they heard at Pentecost.

pos: n. (the peninsula of Rome; the destination of Paul's appeal and of his last voyage)
etymology: Latin Italia. In the New Testament the name marks a direction rather than a culture — the place the gospel was travelling toward from the day Paul said he must also see Rome.
biblical_def: Italy enters Acts through an expulsion: “a certain Jew named Aquila, born in Pontus, lately come from Italy, with his wife Priscilla; (because that Claudius had commanded all Jews to depart from Rome)” (Act 18:2). It returns as a sentence: “when it was determined that we should sail into Italy, they delivered Paul and certain other prisoners unto one named Julius, a centurion of Augustus' band” (Act 27:1), and “the centurion found a ship of Alexandria sailing into Italy; and he put us therein” (Act 27:6). After shipwreck, brethren were found on the road and “so we went toward Rome” (Act 28:14). The epistle to the Hebrews closes with a greeting from there: “They of Italy salute you” (Heb 13:24).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a centurion as a military officer among the Romans who commanded a hundred men, and a prisoner as one who is confined in a prison or held in custody.
webster_full: CENTURION, n. Among the Romans, a military officer who commanded a hundred men, a centenary or century.
PRISONER, n. One who is confined in a prison by legal arrest or warrant; also, a person under arrest or in custody.
APPEAL, n. In law, the removal of a cause or suit from an inferior to a superior tribunal.
scriptures: Act 18:2
And found a certain Jew named Aquila, born in Pontus, lately come from Italy, with his wife Priscilla; (because that Claudius had commanded all Jews to depart from Rome:) and came unto them.
Act 27:1
And when it was determined that we should sail into Italy, they delivered Paul and certain other prisoners unto one named Julius, a centurion of Augustus' band.
Where we found brethren, and were desired to tarry with them seven days: and so we went toward Rome.
Salute all them that have the rule over you, and all the saints. They of Italy salute you.
corruption_summary: An emperor's expulsion order put Aquila and Priscilla in Corinth exactly when Paul arrived there, which is how Acts tells the story of providence.
corruption_paragraphs: Acts 18:2 gives a persecution and a provision in one sentence. Claudius commanded all Jews to depart from Rome; Aquila and Priscilla, therefore, were in Corinth, of the same craft as Paul, when he came there alone and with little money. They housed him, worked with him, travelled with him to Ephesus, taught Apollos the way of God more perfectly, and hosted a church in their house. An imperial edict aimed at scattering a people delivered the two co-workers Paul most needed to the exact city where he needed them.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the one Paul stated from Rome itself: the things which happened unto me have fallen out rather unto the furtherance of the gospel. He had wanted to see Rome for years and arrived as a prisoner after a shipwreck, and the palace guard heard the gospel as a result. Acts ends with him in his own hired house, preaching the kingdom of God with all confidence, no man forbidding him — and the last word of the book in Greek is that adverb, unhinderedly. The chain was real. It did not slow the word.
roots_lines: Greek akolutos (G209) — without hindrance, freely; Acts 28:31 only.
usage: “Lately come from Italy” — an expulsion that supplied Paul with fellow workers.
“We should sail into Italy” — the apostle delivered to a centurion.
“They of Italy salute you” — a church in the capital.

pos: n. (the Greek name for Edom; the land of Esau's descendants, standing under a particular judgment)
etymology: Greek Idoumaia, from Hebrew Edom, red — the name Esau earned over a bowl of red pottage. The nation and the birthright sale carry the same word.
biblical_def: Isaiah makes Idumea the type of the nations under the sword: “my sword shall be bathed in heaven: behold, it shall come down upon Idumea, and upon the people of my curse, to judgment” (Isa 34:5), “for the LORD hath a sacrifice in Bozrah, and a great slaughter in the land of Idumea” (Isa 34:6), and gives the reason: “it is the day of the LORD'S vengeance, and the year of recompences for the controversy of Zion” (Isa 34:8). Ezekiel names the specific offence: “As thou didst rejoice at the inheritance of the house of Israel, because it was desolate, so will I do unto thee” (Eze 35:15).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines vengeance as the infliction of pain on another in return for an injury or offense, and when used of God, the just retribution of punishment.
webster_full: VENGEANCE, n. The infliction of pain on another, in return for an injury or offense. Such infliction, when it proceeds from malice, is revenge, and morally wrong; when the infliction proceeds from justice, it is vengeance, and lawful.
RECOMPENSE, n. An equivalent returned for any thing given, done or suffered; compensation; reward; requital.
CONTROVERSY, n. Dispute; debate; agitation of contrary opinions; also, in Scripture, a cause pleaded.
scriptures: Isa 34:5
For my sword shall be bathed in heaven: behold, it shall come down upon Idumea, and upon the people of my curse, to judgment.
Isa 34:8
For it is the day of the LORD'S vengeance, and the year of recompences for the controversy of Zion.

As thou didst rejoice at the inheritance of the house of Israel, because it was desolate, so will I do unto thee: thou shalt be desolate, O mount Seir, and all Idumea, even all of it: and they shall know that I am the LORD.
Oba 1:10
For thy violence against thy brother Jacob shame shall cover thee, and thou shalt be cut off for ever.
corruption_summary: Edom is judged for standing on the other side in the day of his brother's calamity, and Obadiah names the sin as violence against a brother.
corruption_paragraphs: Obadiah is one chapter long and it is entirely about this. Edom did not sack Jerusalem; Edom watched. Thou stoodest on the other side, in the day that the strangers carried away captive his forces; thou shouldest not have looked on the day of thy brother in the day that he became a stranger; neither shouldest thou have rejoiced over the children of Judah in the day of their destruction. Ezekiel says the same — as thou didst rejoice at the inheritance of the house of Israel, because it was desolate, so will I do unto thee. The gladness of a bystander is charged as violence against a brother.

The corruption to name is the conviction that spectatorship is innocent. Edom's hands did not open the gate, and Edom is cut off for ever. Proverbs 24:17-18 legislates for the same heart in private life: rejoice not when thine enemy falleth, and let not thine heart be glad when he stumbleth, lest the LORD see it, and it displease him. Behind the whole account lies a birthright sold for one morsel of meat, of which Hebrews 12:16 warns the church directly. Idumea in the prophets is not merely a neighbouring state; it is what a man's descendants become when he despises what God gave him and hates the brother who received it.
roots_summary: Hebrew Edom (H123), red, Edom; Seir (H8165), the mountain of Edom; naqam (H5359), vengeance; rib (H7379), controversy, cause.
roots_lines: Hebrew Edom (H123) — Edom, Idumea; Isaiah 34:5, Genesis 25:30, Obadiah 1:1.
Hebrew rib (H7379) — controversy, cause, suit; Isaiah 34:8, Micah 6:2.
usage: “It shall come down upon Idumea, and upon the people of my curse” — Isaiah's sword.
“As thou didst rejoice… so will I do unto thee” — the sentence fits the sin.
“For thy violence against thy brother Jacob” — Obadiah's charge.

pos: n. (Greece; in Daniel the third of the four kingdoms, named centuries before it rose)
etymology: Latin Graecia. The KJV uses Grecia for the Hebrew and Aramaic Yavan, Javan, the son of Japheth whose descendants settled the Aegean.
biblical_def: Daniel is given the interpretation outright: “the rough goat is the king of Grecia: and the great horn that is between his eyes is the first king” (Dan 8:21), and the sequel — “that being broken, whereas four stood up for it, four kingdoms shall stand up out of the nation, but not in his power” (Dan 8:22). The angel names it as a power still to come: “the prince of Grecia shall come” (Dan 10:20). And chapter eleven begins the detailed account: “there shall stand up yet three kings in Persia; and the fourth… shall stir up all against the realm of Grecia” (Dan 11:2). The scheme was set in chapter two: “another third kingdom of brass, which shall bear rule over all the earth” (Dan 2:39).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a kingdom as the territory or country subject to a king, and prophecy as a foretelling; prediction; a declaration of something to come.
webster_full: KINGDOM, n. The territory or country subject to a king; an undivided territory under the dominion of a king or monarch.
PROPHECY, n. A foretelling; prediction; a declaration of something to come. As God only knows future events with certainty, no being but God can utter a real prophecy.
MONARCHY, n. A state or government in which the supreme power is lodged in the hands of a single person.
scriptures: Dan 2:39
And after thee shall arise another kingdom inferior to thee, and another third kingdom of brass, which shall bear rule over all the earth.
Dan 8:21
And the rough goat is the king of Grecia: and the great horn that is between his eyes is the first king.
Dan 8:22
Now that being broken, whereas four stood up for it, four kingdoms shall stand up out of the nation, but not in his power.
Dan 11:2

And now will I shew thee the truth. Behold, there shall stand up yet three kings in Persia; and the fourth shall be far richer than they all: and by his strength through his riches he shall stir up all against the realm of Grecia.
corruption_summary: Daniel names Grecia and describes the break-up of its empire into four while Babylon still stood and Persia had not yet fallen.
corruption_paragraphs: Daniel 8:21-22 is precise enough to be embarrassing to unbelief. The rough goat is the king of Grecia; the great horn is the first king; that horn is broken at the height of its strength and four kingdoms stand up in its place, but not in his power. Alexander died at thirty-two and his empire was divided among four of his generals. Daniel wrote in the sixth century, in the reign of Belshazzar, with Babylon still standing. Chapter 2 had already laid the frame — gold, silver, brass, iron — and the stone cut without hands that breaks them all and fills the whole earth.

The corruption to name is the late-dating of Daniel, which the critical schools have maintained since Porphyry in the third century for one stated reason: prophecy this specific must have been written after the events. The argument is circular and its premise is theological rather than historical — it assumes what it claims to prove, that God does not foretell. Christ settled the authorship for the church by citing Daniel the prophet in the Olivet Discourse. Daniel 11:2 begins, now will I shew thee the truth, and the God who says that is the God who declares the end from the beginning.
roots_summary: Hebrew Yavan (H3120), Javan, Greece; Aramaic malku (H4437), kingdom; tsaphir (H6842), he goat.
usage: “The rough goat is the king of Grecia” — named before it rose.
“Four kingdoms shall stand up out of the nation, but not in his power.”
“A third kingdom of brass, which shall bear rule over all the earth.”
